{"docket_number": "98-405", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1998", "first_party": "Reno", "first_party_label": "Appellant", "second_party": "Bossier Parish School Board", "second_party_label": "Appellee", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Appeal", "lower_court": null, "argued": ["1999-04-26T05:00:00Z"], "question": "

Does section 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 prohibit preclearance of a redistricting plan enacted with a discriminatory but nonretrogressive purpose?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act on 1995 prohibits Bossier Parish, Louisiana from enacting any change in a "voting qualification[,] prerequisite[,] standard, practice, or procedure" without first obtaining preclearance from either the Attorney General or the District Court. Following the 1990 census, the District Court granted Bossier Parish preclearance to redistrict. The U.S. Supreme Court, in Reno v. Bossier Parish School Bd., 520 U.S. 471, vacated the court's judgment and remanded for the court to question whether the section 5 purpose inquiry ever extends beyond the search for retrogressive intent. The District Court again granted preclearance. The court found that there was no evidence of discriminatory but nonretrogressive purpose. The court left open the question of whether section 5 prohibits preclearance of a plan enacted with such a purpose.

", "conclusion": "

No. In a 5-4 opinion delivered by Justice Antonin Scalia, the Court held that section 5 does not prohibit preclearance of a redistricting plan enacted with a discriminatory but nonretrogressive purpose. "As we have repeatedly noted, in vote-dilution cases [section 5] prevents nothing but backsliding, and preclearance under [section 5] affirms nothing but the absence of backsliding," wrote Justice Scalia. Justices David H. Souter, John Paul Stevens and Stephen G. Breyer wrote dissenting opinions. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg joined the opinions of Justices Souter and Stevens. "Now executive and judicial officers of the United States will be forced to preclear illegal and unconstitutional voting schemes patently intended to perpetuate discrimination," argued Justice Souter.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear argument next to number 98405, Janet Reno versus Bossier Parish School Board and George Price versus Bossier Parish School Board. Spectators are admonished, do not talk until you get out of the courtroom. The Court remains in session. Mr. Wolfson. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, Congress enacted Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act in 1965 to prevent jurisdictions from contriving voting practices with the purpose of perpetuating official discrimination and prolonging the existing disparity between Black and White voter participation at that time. The background and the text of Section 5 and this Court's decisions construing it show that it reaches all voting changes enacted with a discriminatory purpose and it is not limited to changes intended to make matters worse for minorities. Particularly persuasive on this point is the background of Section 5, which confirms that it reaches all intentionally discriminatory voting changes. A principal target of Section 5 was hard-bitten official resistance to increase Black voter participation and evasion by covered jurisdictions of adverse Federal Court decrees that had declared such resistance to be unconstitutional. In 1965, Congress was concerned with opening up the process to increase Black participation and not just preventing further encroachment on Black's registration and right to vote. Why would it be concerned about only that purpose and not also that effect? In other words, you may be right about this, but if you're right about it, we just made a wrong decision when we said that the effect portion only covers retrogression. Well, we're — But once you've made that decision, it seems to me the purpose clause only covers retrogression. Why would Congress say we don't care if the — if the effect clause only covers retrogression, but we want the purpose clause to cover everything? Why wouldn't it want the effect clause to cover everything? MR. The reason is that Section 5 reaches both the Constitution itself and also goes beyond the Constitution to reach those changes that, although not discriminatory — motivated by a discriminatory purpose, nonetheless have an adverse effect on the — on the ability of minorities to participate. And in Beer, when the Court construed the effect prong, it was — it was considering Congress's decision to go beyond the 14th and 15th Amendment and address only — only changes that had that — that had that effect. In other words, there was no question in that case that Congress had exercised its authority to enforce the 14th and 15th Amendment itself, which reaches — which reaches discriminatory voting changes. The only question was, as was put earlier in this case, how far beyond the Constitution did Congress intend to reach? Now, and the — that was reaffirmed in City of Rome, where the Court once again said — looked at the effect prong. It was challenged there as being beyond Congress's power to enforce — enforce the 14th and 15th Amendment. And the Court said, yes, it's true, the effect prong does reach beyond the Constitution, but it — it nonetheless upheld as a valid exercise of Congress's power. MR. Do we even reach this question, Mr. Wolfson, if the district court's findings of fact are upheld? MR. The district court — we read the — although it is unclear — MR. You would have to show they're clearly erroneous, I would. MR. No, I'll — I don't — I don't agree with that. Although it is unclear, we read the district court as making findings of fact in — in the traditional sense only on the question of retrogressive purpose and not really reaching the issue of a discriminatory but not a retrogressive purpose. MR. What — what — what — what if you're wrong on that question? MR. Well, even if the district court did opine on the subject of — of it, it didn't look at the question of discriminatory — the broader question — under the Arlington Heights standard. So it — there is no finding of fact which — MR. Well, how can you — how can you tell that it didn't? MR. Well, it didn't — excuse me — it didn't — it certainly didn't examine any of the evidence under Arlington Heights with a view towards discriminatory but non-retrogressive intent. Each time it looked at — each time it recited an Arlington Heights factor and then sifted the evidence, it then said — and — and then this doesn't show retrogressive intent. And one of the most important findings of — or observations was it made — that it made, this court on the previous case had remanded the case specifically so that the district court could look at the importance of the history of resistance to school desegregation decrees. And when the district court recited that point, it then said all of this evidence is admissible to show intent, but nonetheless it doesn't show retrogressive intent. So it — it clearly understood that that evidence should be — should be concerned about discriminatory but non-retrogressive intent. But nonetheless, the only way that it evaluated it referred to retrogressive intent. MR. I thought it says the opposite. I mean, I thought the first opinion — it says plaintiff bears the burden of proving it did not adopt the police-jury plan with a discriminatory purpose. Then you in your brief say, we argued discriminatory purpose. Then on remand, the majority says, we don't have to go into this purpose business because the record will not support a conclusion that extends beyond the presence or absence of retrogressive relief. MR. MR. But it — MR. Then Judge Silberman says in his concurrence, we, of course, never rejected such evidence, the evidence being that — MR. Right. But it's difficult — that sentence that Your Honor just quoted, it's difficult in — in — I believe impossible to square that with — with several things. First of all, the sentence where it says all of that history is admissible to prove intent. So plainly, the district court — although at one point the district court said the record doesn't — doesn't appear to suggest evidence, we don't — we can't — we might be able to imagine that there might be facts of discriminatory intent, yet clearly two pages later understands that that's this case and that there is evidence to support discriminatory but non-retrogressive intent. MR. And frankly, initially from your thing, I did think maybe they didn't consider this. But looking at these statements again, I — I would think a fair reading of it was that we looked at all the evidence and we think there isn't discriminatory — MR. Well, the question — the question — the district court then went on to say, of course — excuse me, I have a little problem — a throat problem. The question we will answer is whether the record disproves Bossier Parish's retrogressive intent. MR. And that proceeds to go through the Arlington Hives's — MR. That's because they thought they already decided that there is no discriminatory purpose, and since there is no discriminatory purpose, they don't have to get to the question that interested us, which is whether you have to have a discriminatory purpose. MR. Well, it — it would be easy to understand if it had done the other way, which is we — there might be discriminatory purpose, but it doesn't go — it's not so bad as to be retrogressive. MR. No, no. MR. I thought — MR. MR. I thought that the discriminatory intent in this case — the government did not argue that it was a retrogressive intent. MR. Our entire theory of this case was that the intent of Bossier Parish School Board was to hold the line as much as possible against further black participation in the — in the affairs of the school board. MR. So all of the evidence that went to retrogressive intent was, by definition, evidence that went to — it had to be, by definition, evidence that went to discriminatory intent. It's not — it wouldn't be really possible to even examine the question of retrogressive intent without considering discriminatory intent. MR. I mean, if you're trying to make — MR. But I think what I'm worried about — and I'll say — and maybe — I'll say it again, because maybe — I'm worried that on rereading this, a fair reading of their opinion is, we understand the government is saying that the Board had a discriminatory purpose for getting retrogression. MR. Let's see whether it did. Two judges think it did not. One judge thinks it did. And therefore, the question before us would be not the general question. Can you be guilty under this statute without a retrogressive intent but with a retrogressive purpose? Because this case doesn't present that question unless we were to find that it did have a retrogressive — uh, discriminatory. MR. Well, we would submit that the — what the District Court — of course, the District Court ultimately found what I'd call a legal conclusion, which is that there was no purpose to deny or abridge the right to vote. In reaching that conclusion, this Court had previously remanded for an application of the Arlington Heights factors. In following that remand, in reaching that conclusion, it applied the Arlington Heights factors only to consider whether there was retrogressive intent. So even if it did have a view about what — about whether there was a discriminatory intent, it's not the sort of finding or ruling that is entitled to Rule 52, a deference under the clearly erroneous standard, because it didn't apply the appropriate legal framework to the record in the case. Now, it was never our theory that there was a retrogressive intent, because it was entirely the understanding of the case that — that as is entire — as is — as how we read Section 5, the main purpose of Section 5 — or I should say a principle purpose of Section 5 — was to stop the — the situation where a jurisdiction simply replaced one discriminatory voting change with another — voting law with another, entitled really to hold the line or perhaps to retrench a little bit, little bit, bit by bit, and draw out constantly the process of — of black — of increased black participation and — and — and — and — and delay and delay and delay. And Congress reaffirmed that, if I — if I may turn — Congress reaffirmed that in — in 1970 and in 1975 and in 1982, when each time it recognized that jurisdictions having recognized that they simply — you know, it was simply unacceptable to prevent blacks from registering altogether, they tried new devices. They started the process of intentional vote dilution, of changing to at-large — at-large district — I assume all those things are open to challenge under Section 2. They certainly are. They certainly are. But of course — And under Section 2, however, the burden of proof is on the plaintiff. That's — that's — that's absolutely correct. But one of the purposes of Section 5 — But you would say that in this very case, a Section 2 challenge could be mounted? I believe it could be. But of course — But it hasn't. It has not. But one of the benefits of Section 5 that Congress anticipated or understood was that Section 2 challenges and affirmative Constitution litigation wouldn't have to be brought, understanding, A, that it's — obviously it's expensive and — Well, if you're correct, I suppose Section 2 would fall into disuse. No, no, because it has to be — there has to be intentional — in a situation like this, it has to be intentional vote dilution. Section 2 critically doesn't require that element of intent on an affirmative — on an affirmative case showing vote dilution. So — But what happened to the argument in your brief that it would be horrible if — if Federal courts should have to approve under Section 5 schemes that are unconstitutional? And that — You — you — you acknowledge that some schemes that are unconstitutional will be approved under Section 5, namely those in which there may be a violation of the Constitution which is not — which is not an intentional one within the meaning of Section 5. Well, it's — it's not an intentional one. Well, of course — I — I may not be understanding correctly, but Mobile v. Bolden and then Rogers v. Lodge seem to indicate that proof of a discriminatory purpose is required to establish a violation of the 14th and 15th Amendment. Well, then your answer to Justice O'Connor has to be changed. Well, no, speak — Section 2 — in affirmative Section 2 litigation doesn't require a showing of intent. I mean, in Thornburg v. Jingles, the Court made clear that it — it can be — and, and, of course, when Congress re-amended — amended the Statute in 1982, made clear that a Section 2 violation may be made showing on a — solely on a showing of a dilutive impact of the plan. But when the — the Justice Department — But if you would then have to, in some instances, give approval under Section 5 if it had a dilutive impact, yet no proof of discriminatory purpose. That's — that is correct, and it's the clear consequence of the Court's earlier decision in — in — in Bossier — in Bossier 1. That is, if it — if it solely has a dilutive — if it solely has a dilutive impact, no intent, and that impact is not retrogressive, then it — there is neither the purpose nor the effect of — of denying or abridging the right to vote. Now, that's — Would you have to give preclearance to a plan that violated the First Amendment? The Attorney General does not review plans for violation of the Fifth Amendment. Well, but, again, this goes to Justice Scalia's point. You said, oh, well, you can't approve — Well, no, not — Of course — It's unconstitutional, and — And — and we're — we're trying — we're trying to test that. Right. Because under your — your view — Excuse me. Excuse me. Under — under — under your view, you would have — have Section 5 do all the work of Section 2 — No — In — in — in order to avoid — this — Circumstance that you confront us with — of — of — of the Department of Justice having to approve an unconstitutional plan. But it seems to me that that would happen in — in — in — in various instances. Well, the statute does say denying or abridging the right to vote on account of color, race, language, minority. And its background, as well, shows that it was intended to enforce the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendment, at least its guarantees against discrimination on account of race and color. And it — it plainly — it was written and was plainly intended to enforce at the very — at the beginning, the Fifteenth Amendment as well. Now, the Fourteenth Amendment, it does include discriminant vote — intentional vote dilution claims. It — it — it also includes one person, one vote. And — and preclearance courts don't generally review a plan solely because it might not comply with one person, one vote. Oh, but it does — it does eliminate some of the — you know, the instinctive reaction. My, will a Court have to approve something that is unconstitutional? There's — it's no doubt that, in some instances, the Section 5 procedure envisions a Court approving something that's unconstitutional. All it's saying is it is not unlawful in this respect. Well, it's — And doesn't Section 5 itself refer to — to other challenges, to — to a Section 2 proceeding? Yes, but — And you think that — that it refers to them only for that narrow class of cases that you described? Well, it — it — it — it — section — an enforcement proceeding under Section 2 and Section 5 is also an enforcement relating to denying or abridging or having the result of such on account of race or color. It's — Section 2 doesn't assimilate the First Amendment and permit a — a First Amendment challenge to a — a — a voting change. However, Congress's intent, again, in enacting Section 5 was to enforce the 14th and 15th Amendments. Now, of course, in a — in a preclearance case, there may be a First Amendment concern out there, but it's unlikely that there is going to be evidence brought to the Court's attention that might — you know, would bear directly on a First Amendment challenge. But in a — in a — in a Section 5 case, there's likely to be extensive evidence that the — the change was enacted with the intent to discriminate against minorities. And yet, under the Board's submission, as long as — you know, essentially, non-retrogression creates a safe harbor for that intentional discrimination. As long as we can say, well, it's true that — you know, it's true that we intended to discriminate, but we intend — didn't intend to make anything worse than that — than preclearances — and we didn't make anything worse — than preclearances required. It's difficult to believe that the Congress that enacted the Voting Rights Act in 1965 and then reenacted it three times, and with the reenactment, also directed its specific attention to the problem of intentional vote dilution, recognizing that, yes, Blacks were formally being allowed to cast a ballot. So in that sense — they were registering to vote, so in that sense there had been an amelioration, but nonetheless the — the devices were being arranged to prevent those votes from being — from literally being effective, and intentionally so. Mr. Wilson, I — I want to get clear on what you think the burden is. As I understand it, you take the position that if it is clear from the evidence that goes in in the Section 5 proceeding that there would be an intent to discriminate, that there cannot be Section 5 approval, if it's obvious. MR. Not just if it's — I mean — not just if it's clear. That is, we do take the position that the jurisdiction does have the burden of proof on it — MR. Well, that was going to be my next question. But certainly — MR. Does the jurisdiction have the burden to prove, affirmatively, not only that there would be no retrogression, but that there is no intent to dilute? MR. Yes, but — MR. All right. I mean, that doesn't mean that it has — it's a burden that's impossible to meet. MR. Well, make — time is short, so forgive me for interrupting you. If — if you are right on the burden of proof, then was the District Court wrong here because it made no affirmative finding with respect to that burden? It, in effect — I think that you could read the District Court as saying, we can't find that there was an affirmative intent to dilute. MR. But the issue it should have addressed, on your view, is, was there a showing by the District that there was no intent to dilute? MR. Absolutely. And — and — and it did not make that — it did not make that finding. It passed by this entire issue quite rapidly. I'd like to reserve the remainder of my time for rebuttal. MR. Thank you, Mr. Wolfson. Ms. — Ms. Brannon, we'll hear from you. MS. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. Mr. Price and the other defendant interveners are back before the Court today because they have been trying for seven years to have the Bossier Parish School Board adopt a non-discriminatory reapportionment — MR. On that, could I just — because — could I — because you know the record well on this. Yes. MR. I found in the question Justice Souter just asked, in the first opinion, the Court says plaintiff, i.e. the Board, bears the burden of proving that it did not adopt the police jury plan with a discriminatory purpose. MS. Yes. MR. Your Honor, we — Your Honor, we — — what's the problem with that? MS. Your Honor, we agree that that is an accurate statement of the burdens of proof. But we think that what happened on the remand is that the Court — and I'm referring here to Appendix Page 3A, to the Appendix to the Jurisdictional Statement — when the Court framed up the legal issue before it began any analysis of the evidence at all — and it said ultimately three things — we know three things it said that we — I think can all understand — that it won't deal with the legal issue of intent to retrogress versus discriminatory intent that this Court had asked it to deal with on remand, that the question it would answer — this is at the top of 4A — is whether the record disproves Bossier Parish's retrogressive intent. And then, as it applied the Arlington Heights factors, that's the factual analysis. It then limited itself. MR. It did. You're absolutely right. But the reason that it did is it said to go into the discriminatory purpose, not discriminatory non-retrogressive purpose question, would require imagined facts. It says we can imagine facts where that would be an issue, but that isn't the case before us. So I assume that what it's doing is simply referring back to its first opinion, where it said, we find on the facts, giving the burden of proof to the Board, that the Board has borne the burden of proof and there is no discriminatory purpose. And that's how — I mean, I — I want to be fair to the district court. And if it's — that's — that's, of course, what your opponents will say it said. So I want to — you — you to explain why that isn't what it meant. MS. Because, Your Honor, on 3A, the closest language we have, just before the passage you referenced about imagined facts, it said, the record will not support a conclusion that extends beyond the presence or absence of retrogressive intent. That does not sound like a fact-finding, that there is no discriminatory purpose beyond retrogressive intent. It's the definition of the issue. Well, why doesn't — why — Well, why doesn't it? When they say the record won't support a finding, that would be my idea, in a way, of a precise fact-finding. in a way of a precise fact-finding. Your Honor, because it follows the words with the presence or the absence, as if the parties never addressed the issue. And, in fact, the whole case was never about retrogression. We stipulated retrogression away before we started. Do we usually parse a district court's findings and conclusions quite this minutely? I mean, there's really a presumption in favor of a district court's findings of fact. Your Honor, and we agree. And with all respect to the district court, of course, in this process, there's no intermediate court of appeals to sort some of this, so you're reviewing directly the trial court decision. Am I right that you did not ask to reopen the record? No one asked to reopen the record. Am I right that you did not ask to reopen it? That's correct. When it speaks of neither presence nor absence, isn't it saying that on the evidence, we are left in a total state of equipoise regardless of who has the burden? Your Honor, I think it is making some kind of a statement that the issue simply is not present in the record. And, in fact, that just cannot be the case. Well, they couldn't have — I was going to say, they couldn't have meant that because of the evidence that went in. So isn't it fair to read it as saying, in effect, regardless of who has the burden here, the evidence leaves us really in equipoise? We can't say there was. We can't say there wasn't. Which, in this case, Justice Souter, if that is a fair reading, the judgment should be reversed. The board here had the burden of proof. And in fact — So equipoise will not do it if it had the burden. Yes. And equipoise will lead to reversal. Where does it say equipoise? I thought that it — that it — what he's saying — Souter said equipoise. So if the — if the record — I mean, we don't do this with — Look, I mean, there's an elephant in the room. The issue is the elephant, all right? And here everybody talks and never mentions it. Well, I mean, they're not that unaware. The whole issue in this case is discriminatory purpose. Your Honor — So if he says — Yes, Justice Breyer, but there are two elephants. One is a retrogressive purpose, and the other is non-retrogressive discriminatory purpose. They talked about the former, but not the latter. And only reach the one. And in some assumption at the start of the opinion, didn't reach the other. And I would also point out, Justice Breyer, that there are findings on page 7A of the appendix that cannot be squared with some finding that there was no discriminatory purpose. The Court found — I quote, The evidence rather clearly establishes that the Board did not welcome improvement in the position — Where on 7A are you reading from, Ms. B. I am on page 7A, Your Honor. At the bottom of the page, about six lines up. Thank you. This is with respect to departure from normal practices. The evidence establishes rather clearly that the Board did not welcome improvement in the position of racial minorities with respect to their effective exercise of the electoral franchise. Now, Arlington Heights teaches that a discriminatory purpose infecting a governmental decision, even if there are some legitimate purposes that the governmental entity can cite to, invalidates that decision. that the deference that is owed by a federal court to a decision falls away at that point. It's not just another purpose. It's a purpose that's at the core of the Constitution. Excuse me. Does it constitute discriminatory purpose not to welcome something? I mean, is that the burden that non-discrimination imposes upon the Board? Justice Scalia, it's one of three ways on that same page that the District Court talked about what Mr. Wolfson referred to, folding the line. This is a district with no majority black districts in its history, and no elected... What the government says is that they weren't happy with the state of affairs. It doesn't suggest that they took... And, in fact, it would be contrary to the remainder of the opinion to suggest that it said that they, you know, that they had any purpose of preventing that state of affairs. Well, Your Honor, the Court also talks on that same page in the connection with the school desegregation history about the Board's tenacious determination to maintain the status quo, and it also talks about powerful support for the proposition that the school board, in fact, resisted adopting a redistricting plan that would have created majority black districts. Excuse me, the tenacious determination... I'm sorry, Chief. Go ahead. Certainly that's not inconsistent with the sort of finding that would support affirmance here. Your Honor, standing alone, I don't think it would be, but in the context of this record in which there were irregularities in procedure, a whole year of knowing that the police jury plan was there and pre-cleared, and the Board only rushed to that plan when one thing happened, when it's on map that showed... But, okay, you're arguing facts, and you've got to show that the district court's fines were clearly erroneous. Now, are you in the process of doing that now? No, Your Honor, what we're saying is that these findings on page seven demonstrate that what we were referring to earlier on page three is a statement of legal issues and legal conclusions, not of facts, because the two simply cannot be reconciled on this record. And, Your Honor, if I might, with respect to Justice O'Connor's question about Section 2, there are at least three very crucial purposes that are served by Section 2 that simply would not be covered by Section 5 if our view of the reading of Section 5 prevails. One is that Section 2 covers the whole United States, not just covered jurisdictions. It is available to private parties for affirmative litigation, which, of course, Section 5 isn't. We intervened here. And Section 5, of course, covers only changes. Section 2 can be used to attack voting practices that have been in effect for 50 years. So we think that Section 2 is both are crucial, can be read together and very consistently, reading purpose the way we read purpose. The final point I'd like to make is that a reading of the purpose clause to be coextensive with the Constitutional protection that this Court really called into play when it commended Arlington Heights on remand makes sense. For example, if the Board here had barred black citizens from its public meetings on this plan, had hurled racial epithets at them, had said, we will never let you people elect someone in this district, we would still be at a point of having to preclear this if the test is retrogression because this is not retrogression. To me, our first responsibility is not to make sense of the law. The first responsibility is to follow the text of the law. And I find it very difficult to overcome the obstacle that the law says does not have the purpose and will not have the effect of X. And what you're arguing is that that means does not have the purpose, does not have the effect of X, but does not have the purpose of Y. Yes, Your Honor. I don't know of any other instance in, not just in the United States Code, in human expression where you say does not have the purpose and effects of X and you mean one thing for purpose and another for effect. Do you have any other example? Your Honor, I would commend to the Court page 141 of the Beer decision in which the effect construction was interpreted to be retrogression. The statute says does not have the purpose, that is talking about the present purpose of the governmental decision maker, and will not have the effect, which, as the Court said in Beer, had a predictive quality to it, which is a different measure. Thank you, Ms. Van. We'll hear now from you, Mr. Carvin. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, to begin to follow up on Justice Scalia's last question, I think it's apparent that appellants can't argue that the plain language of the statute as interpreted in the retrogration cases supports their view of Section 5. So I'd like to address directly their broader argument that the goal of Section 5 was to enforce the 15th Amendment and therefore it must prohibit everything that the 15th Amendment prohibits. We agree, certainly, that Congress was using its 15th Amendment enforcement power when it imposed the extraordinary preclearance procedures that it did on covered jurisdictions, but we know for two very fundamental reasons, that it was not incorporating the 15th Amendment substantive prohibition against non-retrogressive discriminatory changes. Most obviously, Section 5 simply cannot remedy non-retrogressive discriminatory changes. It can't reach it. There's a million examples, but a simple one would be, let's assume the covered jurisdiction has a polling place that's six blocks away from the minority neighborhood, and the proposed change is to move it five blocks away. And it's stipulated that they would have moved it four blocks away, more convenient, but for pure racial animals. What is your remedy under Section 5? You deny the change. You deny the move to five blocks from the minority neighborhood, and you reinstate the status quo ante. So now, the polling place is six blocks away from the minority neighborhood.
